description_full: Tsakos Energy Navigation Limited, together with its subsidiaries, provides seaborne crude oil and petroleum product transportation services in Greece and internationally. The company owns and operates various vessels, including VLCC, Suezmax, Aframax, Panamax, Handysize, MR, LNG carrier, and shuttle DP2 tankers. It also provides marine transportation services for national, major, and other independent oil companies and refiners. The company was formerly known as MIF Limited and changed its name to Tsakos Energy Navigation Limited in July 2001. Tsakos Energy Navigation Limited was incorporated in 1993 and is based in Athens, Greece.
ceo_bio: Dr. Nikolas P. Tsakos Ph.D. | Founder, CEO & Director | Age 62
financial_summary: Tsakos Energy Navigation Ltd is a small-cap energy business with a $1.4B market cap on $799M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +2.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $5M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 28% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 112% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.

val: The stock trades 52% below its DCF fair value of $93.74, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 52%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $62.16 to $140 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 4.5 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 127% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of -0.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $62.50 on average, 39% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.20).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.85x.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 14pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.5x net debt to EBITDA ($293.3M of cash against $1.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.05 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.95 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.5% over 3 years, 4.4% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
At current returns, reinvesting 33% of profits supports about 2.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (37.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 3, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 28.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 36%.
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 4 sales over the past year, net $103K sold.
It returns 4.4% a year to shareholders (4.5% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years, raising it 5.2% a year over the last five.
